content: Prunus virginiana, commonly referred to as bitter-berry, chokecherry, Virginia bird cherry, or western chokecherry (and sometimes black chokecherry for the variety P. virginiana var. demissa), is a species of bird cherry belonging to the Prunus subgenus Padus. It is native to North America, with its natural range spanning most of Canada (excluding Yukon, Nunavut, and Labrador), the majority of the United States (including Alaska but excluding parts of the southeastern states), and northern Mexico (specifically Sonora, Chihuahua, and Baja California). Chokecherry typically grows as a suckering shrub or a small tree, reaching heights of up to 30 feet. Its leaves are oval-shaped, elongated, and have coarsely serrated edges. The flowers appear in racemes during late spring, well after the leaves have emerged. The fruits, which are technically drupes, are small, measuring about 1 cm in diameter. They vary in color from bright red to black and have a highly astringent taste, being both somewhat sour and bitter. When fully ripe, the fruits become darker in color, less astringent, and slightly sweeter compared to their unripe, red counterparts. The term chokeberry (genus Aronia) is often confused with chokecherry due to the similarity in their names. However, chokecherries belong to the Prunus genus, while chokeberries are part of the Photinia genus. Chokecherries are rich in antioxidant pigments, particularly anthocyanins, a characteristic they share with chokeberries, which adds to the confusion between the two. There are three main varieties of Prunus virginiana: Prunus virginiana var. virginiana (eastern chokecherry) Prunus virginiana var. demissa (western chokecherry) Prunus virginiana var. melanocarpa (wild chokecherry) The wild chokecherry is often considered a nuisance because it serves as a host for tent caterpillars, which can harm other fruit plants. However, cultivated varieties such as 'Goertz' are appreciated for their non-astringent and palatable fruits. Research at the University of Saskatchewan is focused on developing new cultivars to enhance production and processing. Chokecherry is closely related to the black cherry (Prunus serotina) of eastern North America. It can be distinguished from black cherry by its smaller size (black cherry trees can grow up to 100 feet tall), smaller leaves, and sometimes red ripe fruit. The leaves of chokecherry are finely serrated, dark green on the upper surface, and paler underneath, whereas black cherry leaves have blunt edges and are dark green and smooth. The name chokecherry has also been used for the related Manchurian cherry or Amur cherry (Prunus maackii). For many Native American tribes in the Northern Rockies, Northern Plains, and boreal forest regions of Canada and the United States, chokecherries were a vital fruit in their diets. The fruit can be used to make jams, jellies, or syrups, but its bitter nature requires the addition of sugar to make it more palatable. Chokecherry is toxic to horses, moose, cattle, goats, deer, and other ruminant animals, especially after the leaves have wilted (e.g., following frost or branch breakage), as wilting releases cyanide and makes the plant sweeter. Ingesting 10–20 pounds of foliage can be fatal. Symptoms of poisoning in horses include heavy breathing, agitation, and weakness. In 2007, Governor John Hoeven of North Dakota signed a bill designating chokecherry as the official state fruit, partly because its remains have been found at more archaeological sites in the Dakotas than anywhere else. Chokecherry is also used to produce wine, particularly in the western United States (notably in the Dakotas and Utah) and in Manitoba, Canada.
